item.title: FARSim: a fast RF-chain-aware trigger-screening surrogate for radio detection of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays
item.description: arXiv:2605.28373v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Radio arrays provide a scalable route to detecting extensive air showers from ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, but trigger studies for candidate layouts are expensive when every energy, arrival direction, core position and trigger configuration is evaluated with full radio simulations. We present FARSim, a fast surrogate framework that reuses a reduced library of ZHAireS reference footprints to reconstruct ground-plane radio emission and to estimate trigger-relevant observables. The method combines vector geomagnetic and charge-excess field decomposition, geomagnetic-angle and energy scaling, geometrical projection, contour-based core sampling and event-rate integration. We evaluate an independent validation set of 1999 ZHAireS showers; 941 events satisfy the predefined radial-support and station-count requirements and yield a median event-level relative RMSE of 9.4% and a median Pearson coefficient $r_{\mathrm{P}}=0.965$ for the reconstructed geomagnetic lateral profiles. We further extend the peak-field surrogate to time-domain electric-field synthesis by combining the predicted three-component peak-field vector with geometry-dependent normalized pulse templates. Propagating these traces through an RF-chain response enables voltage-domain threshold and L1-trigger diagnostics. When evaluated at the true peak amplitude, the time-domain extension reaches a median vector-waveform $R^2$ of 0.986 over 2112 ZHAireS traces held out from pulse-shape model fitting. FARSim is therefore intended as a rapid, physics-informed screening layer for array-layout and trigger studies; absolute exposure predictions and detector commissioning remain the role of full end-to-end simulations.

item.title: Setting requirements on out-of-band rejection for next-generation CMB experiments. Application to the LiteBIRD instrument
item.description: arXiv:2606.31778v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Next-generation cosmic microwave background experiments have very stringent constraints to achieve the required sensitivity to target polarization $B$ modes. In this work, we intend to set requirements on the out-of-band rejection level, with out-of-band referring to frequencies outside the telescope band-pass. The method developed is applied to the LiteBIRD Medium and High Frequency Telescopes. In order to determine the impact of out-of-band power, we model the instrument's optical response and the spectral emissions of the sky and of the instrument itself. This allows us to propagate optical power inside the telescope. Using this tool, we address both the impact of out-of-band power on the detection chain and on the thermal heat load, together with the impact on the process of separation between astrophysical components. The role of additional static power as well as dynamic power variations is studied. The requirement derived consist in attenuation factors (in dB) in frequency subdomains. They will be used to design the telescopes filters.

item.title: Environmental Noise Challenges for the Einstein Telescope - A Review
item.description: arXiv:2608.07633v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Einstein Telescope (ET) will be a next-generation ground based interferometric gravitational-wave detector designed to explore the Universe to an unprecedented depth and detail. With its 10-15 km long arms, underground infrastructure, and advanced cryogenic technologies to suppress thermal noise, ET aims at achieving a sensitivity up to eight orders of magnitude better than current detectors such as Virgo, LIGO, and KAGRA. The coverage of the low-frequency band, starting at 2 Hz, will enable the observation of earlier inspiral phases of compact binary coalescences, enhancing early-warning capabilities and improving multi-messenger follow-up. However, this increased sensitivity also implies a higher susceptibility to environmental disturbances, particularly in the 2-10 Hz range where anthropogenic, seismic and infrastructural noise noise are most relevant. Therefore, understanding and mitigating environmental contributions are essential to fully exploit the scientific potential of ET. This chapter reviews the ongoing studies on environmental noise for ET, summarizes the main challenges related to site characterization and infrastructure design and outlines the strategies currently under development to ensure optimal detector performance.
item.dc:creator: Matteo Di Giovanni

item.title: Unified matched-filter and excess-power pipeline for gravitational-wave detector characterization
item.description: arXiv:2608.09804v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present sgnax, an open-source pipeline for gravitational-wave detector characterization that produces matched-filter and excess-power transient triggers within a single streaming dataflow graph. Built on the Stream Graph Navigator (sgn) framework, sgnax combines the multi-rate sine-Gaussian matched filtering of snax and the multi-resolution Q-transform of omicron in a Python-native package with shared configuration and output formats. Strain and auxiliary channels share data ingestion and whitening, reducing per-channel processing costs by a factor of 2.8 from one to 32 channels for the Q-transform. A full day of 16 kHz strain is processed in 14 minutes; four processes sharing an NVIDIA V100 analyze 792 auxiliary channels at 1.11 times real-time throughput. The same configuration supports offline and online operation through frame caches, shared memory, and the arrakis distribution service. Matched-filter triggers have approximately five seconds of end-to-end latency, while Q-transform triggers are available within tens of seconds. Injection studies recover 99.4% of recoverable sine-Gaussian signals and show broadband burst recovery consistent with established generators. On 24 hours of LIGO strain, sgnax agrees with production omicron to 0.1% in total trigger count, with per-trigger signal-to-noise ratios agreeing at the percent level across frequency bands. Auxiliary-channel comparisons recover 80% of the snax loud-feature population per time bin. The validation also reveals a multiband amplitude error in production snax that inflates reported signal-to-noise ratios below 25.6 Hz by factors of sqrt(2) to 2.

item.title: DINOspec: Efficient Multimodal Alignment of Vision and Spectral Foundation Models for Astronomy
item.description: arXiv:2608.30503v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Astronomical observations provide multimodal views of physical systems, with images and spectra capturing complementary properties of celestial objects. Scientific foundation models can learn powerful representations from these observations, but representations learned by separate models remain difficult to combine. We investigate whether laten space representations learned by separate vision and spectral models can be aligned without retraining their encoders. We introduce DINOspec, a multimodal framework that aligns a frozen DINOv3 image encoder with a pre-trained AION-1 spectral encoder using lightweight adapters and contrastive learning on 20,472 paired images and spectra of astronomical objects. DINOspec improves galaxy morphology classification (F1: 0.72$\rightarrow$0.78) and spectral type classification (F1: 0.70$\rightarrow$0.74) while training at few as 21M parameters. Redshift prediction shows no consistent improvement over the AION-1 baseline of $R^2\approx0.9$, demonstrating that potential benefits of alignment depends on the configuration and downstream task. These results provide an empirical study of composing astronomical representations from independently pretrained foundation models through lightweight alignment modules.
item.dc:creator: Erica Lastufka, Mariia Drozdova, Daniel Schaerer, Svyatoslav Voloshynovskiy

item.title: Wide Field Localization Using Fixed Modulation Collimators
item.description: arXiv:2609.10384v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rapid, precise localization of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) requires continuous wide-field imaging at hard X-ray and soft gamma-ray energies. We develop a fixed (non-rotating) modulation-collimator architecture to address this challenge. A bigrid collimator, a pair of aligned, periodic slit grids in front of a simple, non-imaging photon-counting detector, transmits an off-axis source through a triangular fringe pattern whose local angular position, the source phase, is recovered from simultaneous count rates in several grid pairs at fixed relative phase offsets, rather than by mechanically rotating a single grid pair as in the classical rotating modulation collimator. Four-phase demodulation of these count rates robustly cancels detector background and grid leakage without requiring rotation. Because the fringe pattern repeats across the sky, a phase measurement corresponds to many candidate source positions; we resolve this ambiguity over an arbitrarily wide field of view using a cascade of progressively coarser-pitched grid stages, generalizing the two-grid vernier-scale technique originally used to localize Sco X-1. This vernier cascade technique reduces the required photon counts and grid-calibration accuracy required to achieve fine angular resolution over a broad field of view. Generalized to two dimensions with orthogonal cascades, the resulting architecture achieves wide-field localization with no moving parts, no time modulation, and only simple photon-counting detectors, a promising candidate for simple, inexpensive, continuous-monitoring instruments supporting time-domain and multi-messenger astrophysics.
item.dc:creator: Steven E. Boggs

item.title: Automatic astrometric calibration of low-cost all-sky cameras
item.description: arXiv:2609.15724v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: All-sky cameras support weather monitoring, amateur astronomy, fireball and space-debris detection, and measurements of light pollution. These applications require reliable astrometric calibration despite imperfect camera alignment and variable observing conditions. We present an open-source procedure that combines a compact fisheye model, an exact rotation to account for camera tilt, and automatic star matching. It can initialise a calibration from a single frame given the observing site coordinates and observation time. We evaluate the procedure on nine cloud-free, moonless frames, obtained with a Raspberry Pi camera and a 1.55 mm lens. Fitting on eight frames and evaluating on the ninth in turn gives a median residual of 0.70 px (95% interval 0.64-0.80 px) across 4172 matches, reduced to 0.60 px by two optional decentering parameters. All nine single-frame calibrations pass the quality criteria and predict positions on other frames with a median residual of 0.77 px. We also apply the clear-sky calibration to 73 frames with varying lunar illumination or cloud cover, obtaining comparable residuals for accepted matches on moonlit frames (0.62 px). These results support reusing a calibration while the camera geometry remains unchanged and enough stars remain visible for reliable matching. To test the generality of the single-frame procedure, we calibrated one night frame from each of 23 different all-sky systems, including fireball-network cameras, observatory sky monitors and amateur stations, with images of 0.3 to 77 megapixels in JPEG, FITS and camera-raw formats. All 23 are calibrated from the site and time alone, with a median fit residual of 0.42 px. Applied to a second frame of the same camera without refitting, the calibrations give a median residual of 0.66 px over 18 systems. The procedure is available as the Python package ascal.

item.title: Characterization of the CSST Survey Camera CCDs: I. basic electro-optical performance
item.description: arXiv:2609.19105v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Chinese Space-station Survey Telescope (CSST) is a flagship mission designed to carry out a large-area high-resolution multiband imaging and slitless spectroscopic survey over a decade. The survey's science drivers, ranging from precision cosmology to stellar astrophysics, impose stringent requirements on the performance of its focal plane detectors. This paper is the first in a series that present ground-based characterization of the 31 flight-model charge-coupled devices (CCDs) of the CSST Survey Camera. Measurements of basic electro-optical performance are reported here. Key results include: full-well capacity $\geq 80\ \mathrm{ke}^{-}$ (limited by the test electronics), non-linearity $<1.4\%$ in the range of $7-70\ \mathrm{ke}^{-}$, median readout noise $3.6\ \mathrm{e}^{-}$, dark current $\leq 0.02\ \mathrm{e}^{-}\mathrm{pix}^{-1}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ at the operating temperature of $-85\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, high quantum efficiency across the survey's spectral range (255-1000 nm), typical pixel response non-uniformity $<1\%$, and charge transfer efficiency $>99.9994\%$ at the flat-field level of $10\ \mathrm{ke}^{-}$. All 31 CCDs meet or exceed the Survey Camera's specifications. These measurements establish a performance baseline and provide inputs for CSST image simulation and data processing pipelines

item.title: Propulsion Systems for a Starshade Rendezvous Mission with the Habitable World Observatory
item.description: arXiv:2610.36200v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We assess how propulsion and operational constraints affect exo-Earth characterization with a starshade rendezvous mission for a Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO)-like telescope at Sun-Earth L2. Using end-to-end Monte Carlo simulations with EXOSIMS, we model a 60 m starshade for visible-band spectroscopy (500-1000 nm) and a 35 m starshade for near-ultraviolet characterization (250-550 nm). For the 60 m design, we compare AEPS Hall, NEXT ion, and Starlink-class Hall thrusters and examine sensitivity to propellant capacity, the fraction of each retargeting slew spent accelerating and decelerating, and on-orbit refueling. With 1000-3000 kg of initial propellant and no refueling, NEXT provides the highest characterization yield: 9-13% more characterizations than AEPS and 13-16% more than the Starlink-class option. Its higher specific impulse enables more retargeting slews per kilogram of propellant. With refueling, yields converge across thruster choices to about 120 cumulative characterizations over 10 years, while propulsion choice mainly affects the number of refueling events. For the 35 m starshade with AEPS, yields are less sensitive to fuel and are dominated by mission duration and geometric accessibility. Increasing the minimum solar keepout angle from 40 to 50 degrees has little effect on yield; increases from 50 to 65 degrees have a modest effect, while angles above 65 degrees rapidly reduce yield, with severe degradation near 80 degrees. These results distinguish fuel-limited and time- or keepout-limited regimes and guide propulsion selection, tank sizing, refueling policy, and keepout constraints for HWO starshade missions.

item.title: Breccia and basalt classification of thin sections of Apollo rocks with deep learning
item.description: arXiv:2410.21024v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Human exploration of the moon is expected to resume in the next decade, following the last such activities in the Apollo programme time. One of the major objectives of returning to the Moon is to continue retrieving geological samples, with a focus on collecting high-quality specimens to maximize scientific return. Tools that assist astronauts in making informed decisions about sample collection activities can maximize the scientific value of future lunar missions. A lunar rock classifier is a tool that can potentially provide the necessary information for astronauts to analyze lunar rock samples, allowing them to augment in-situ value identification of samples. Towards demonstrating the value of such a tool, in this paper, we introduce a framework for classifying rock types in thin sections of lunar rocks. We leverage the vast collection of petrographic thin-section images from the Apollo missions, captured under plane-polarized light (PPL), cross-polarised light (XPL), and reflected light at varying magnifications. Advanced machine learning methods, including contrastive learning, are applied to analyze these images and extract meaningful features. The contrastive learning approach fine-tunes a pre-trained Inception-Resnet-v2 network with the SimCLR loss function. The fine-tuned Inception-Resnet-v2 network can then extract essential features effectively from the thin-section images of Apollo rocks. A simple binary classifier is trained using transfer learning from the fine-tuned Inception-ResNet-v2 to 98.44\% ($\pm$1.47) accuracy in separating breccias from basalts.

item.title: The Atacama Cosmology Telescope: Release of A databaSe of millimeTeR ObservatioNs of Asteroids Using acT ($\mathtt{ASTRONAUT}$)
item.description: arXiv:2508.18300v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present A databaSe of millimeTeR ObservatioNs of Asteroids Using acT ($\mathtt{ASTRONAUT}$) hosted on Amazon Web Services, Inc. (AWS) in the form of a public Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) bucket. This bucket is an Amazon cloud storage database containing flux measurements for a group of asteroids at millimeter (mm) wavelengths. These measurements were collected by the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) from 2017 to 2021 in frequency bands centered near 90, 150, and 220 GHz. The $\mathtt{ASTRONAUT}$ database contains observation times, normalized flux values, and associated error bars for 170 asteroids above a signal-to-noise ratio of 5 for a single frequency band over the stacked co-added maps. We provide an example in generating light curves with this database. We also present a Jupyter notebook to serve as a reference guide when using the S3 bucket. The container and notebook are publicly available in a GitHub repository.

item.title: TransitNet: A Compact Attention-Augmented Deep Learning Framework for Low-SNR Transit Blind Searches
item.description: arXiv:2606.18932v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Motivated by the observational incompleteness of intermediate-to-long-period Earth-size planets, we present TransitNet, a compact attention-augmented deep-learning framework for low-SNR transit blind searches. To enable realistic method development and objective threshold calibration under blind-search conditions, we develop a unified dataset construction, benchmarking, and threshold-selection framework. On recovery benchmarks constructed from unseen Kepler targets, TransitNet attains 95.2 percent accuracy in the challenging SNR range of 6 to 8 and outperforms both TLS and BLS, achieving ROC-AUC and PR-AP values of 0.974 and 0.982, respectively. In an injected Earth-size and sub-Earth-size transit recovery experiment, TransitNet achieves a recovery rate of 93.0 percent, substantially exceeding those of TLS (63.1 percent) and BLS (60.0 percent). In addition to detection, TransitNet provides attention-based estimates of transit windows and midpoints. On an independent evaluation set, 97.4 percent of injected transits are fully covered by the estimated transit window. Applied to real Kepler observations, the model successfully recovers all 34 selected confirmed Kepler planets, with a mean absolute transit midpoint error of 1.24 hours. The model combines a compact footprint of about 1.5 MB with high inference efficiency, yielding speed-ups of about 12 to 25 times relative to CPU-TLS and about 4 to 5 times relative to CPU-BLS. These results demonstrate that TransitNet provides an accurate, scalable, and computationally efficient framework for low-SNR transit blind searches in the tested regime and motivate its extension to longer-period Earth-size planet searches.

item.title: Excursion-set structure factor of the auroral electric field
item.description: arXiv:2606.26854v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A spacecraft crossing the aurora cannot tell whether structures in the field-aligned currents are short-lived or merely small. However, by tracking clusters of coherent radar echoes from aurorae and Fourier-transforming motion-shifted echo pairs across radar snapshots, we can calculate the dynamic structure factor of the point-clouds, thereby quantifying the auroral electric field's spatial power and its persistence from 5 to 40 km, in regions where the radar look-direction is perpendicular to the geomagnetic field. This follows from the fact that coherent E-region radar echoes appear only where the ionospheric electric field exceeds the Farley-Buneman instability threshold, and so a point-target imaging radar naturally samples the field's excursion set; the field's spatiotemporal correlations are discernible from that point process. We find that the echo pattern moves with its cluster: large-scale structures persist for tens of seconds, but scales under 10 km renew within seconds, and conjunctions with Swarm satellite pairs replicate the same scale dependence in field-aligned currents. Coherent radar can thus quantify multi-scale variability in the auroral electric field on Alfv\'enic timescales.

item.title: Addressing Exoplanetary Degeneracies Through Geometry: Application to Asynchronously Rotating Systems
item.description: arXiv:2608.09241v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This study augments the geometry-based InstellCa code that calculates accurate irradiance values to InstellCa--2, which computes the longitude averaged instellation over a given latitude on the planet along with its effective temperature profile. The estimation of instellation is performed considering the planet as a 3D body that asynchronously rotates, causing a varying zenith angle of the star resulting in a diurnal cycle. This serves as a specialised case study to demonstrate how the combination of this relative rotation and extreme proximity to host-stars can affect the estimated effective temperatures of close-in planets. 55 Cancri e is selected specifically to demonstrate the importance of this effect as it has been earlier hypothesised to exhibit asynchronous rotation and also has a debated scientific discourse about the existence of an atmosphere on the planet. The TRAPPIST-1 system, being a multi-planetary system susceptible to mean motion resonances, also serves as an interesting exemplar case to demonstrate these effects. Incorporating the stellar zenith angle to the geometrical analysis allows the possibility of physically feasible Bond albedo values that would otherwise be prohibited if a synchronously rotating bare rock scenario is assumed. Consequently, the degeneracies in the modelling of different atmospheric states of such planets can be reduced if the correct geometry is taken into account.

item.title: The EMA Justitia Probe: Terminator Frame-Based Deployment Orbit Selection and Surface Coverage Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.26581v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Emirates Mission to the Asteroid Belt (EMA) probe is designed to perform asteroid imaging during an uncontrolled ballistic descent to (269) Justitia. The mission design is constrained by main spacecraft proximity operations, uncertain asteroid gravity, limited knowledge of the final deployment trajectory, and requirements for illumination and safe operations. These constraints necessitate a mission design that ensures suitable illumination, attitude determination and control, and payload pointing throughout descent. The EMA probe concept of operations employs near-terminator deployment orbit geometry with continuous Sun visibility and two attitude control modes: single-axis Sun-spin for periodic imaging opportunities and three-axis asteroid-pointing for continuous asteroid visibility. Based on these modes, formal requirements are derived for deployment orbits that enable asteroid observations during ballistic descent. A deployment orbit selection method is developed using the terminator reference frame and a minimum boresight deviation margin. The method identifies families of orbit orientations satisfying illumination and payload observation constraints. Reference orbits are selected and verified through mission geometry analysis and trajectory propagation using a polyhedron gravity model. Asteroid surface coverage is then evaluated for uncontrolled tumbling, Sun-spin, and asteroid-pointing modes. The results characterize the expected imaging performance and demonstrate the feasibility of the EMA probe concept for close-proximity asteroid imaging. The proposed approach can also support future ballistic probe missions subject to similar operational and observational constraints.

item.title: Proposed optimal targets for a Lazuli ExtraSolar Coronagraph reflected starlight exoplanet campaign
item.description: arXiv:2610.31286v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Direct detection and characterization of exoplanet atmospheres via reflected starlight enables probes of composition of mature exoplanet systems (since flux is decoupled from age) at closer separations than via thermal emission (due to observations in visible wavelengths), and even probes of biosignatures. New and upcoming ground and space-based platforms are enabling these observations for the first time. Recently the 3-m Lazuli Space Telescope, from the Eric and Wendy Schmidt Observatory System, was announced, which will be equipped with the ExtraSolar Coronagraph (ESC) designed for reflected light gas giant exoplanet observations in visible wavelengths. In this paper we present 27 known giant exoplanets that could make up an optimal first target list for these observations. This target list spans ages and temperatures of planets not probed before by direct imaging, but some of which will also be accessible to the \textsl{Nancy Grace Roman} Coronagraph instrument and the ELT-METIS thermal imager, providing comprehensive atmosphere characterization and synergies. We discuss the science enabled by ESC observations of this target list and enhancements provided by future astrometric and radial velocity measurements.
